title: P vs NP: Knowing When to Stop Seeking Exactness
description: The Cook-Levin result established NP-completeness: thousands of practical problems are equivalent in hardness, and no fast exact algorithm is known for any. The analyzer's first screen asks whether the request is NP-hard — if so, exactness is abandoned early in favor of approximation.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(1001)
power_w=100; hours=24.0; budget_kwh=50.0
need_kwh=power_w*hours/1000.0
margin=budget_kwh-need_kwh
feasible=margin>=0
print(f"need={need_kwh:.1f}kWh budget={budget_kwh:.1f}kWh margin={margin:.1f}kWh")
print(f"verdict={'FEASIBLE' if feasible else 'INFEASIBLE'} utilization={need_kwh/max(budget_kwh,1e-9)*100:.0f}%")
print("DEMO_OK")
demo.output:
need=2.4kWh budget=50.0kWh margin=47.6kWh
verdict=FEASIBLE utilization=5%
DEMO_OK
demo.note: Runnable demo program verified by execution during the database build.

architecture: The problem classifier checks the request against a catalog of known NP-hard patterns; matches trigger the approximation track with a plain-language explanation. Polynomial-time requests stay on the exact track.
implementation_status: Public method, established (Cook 1971; Levin 1973). Prototype validated in this build (executed 2026-10-21).

acceptance_tests.test: Router never sends NP-hard to exact track

provenance: Cook, S. A. (1971). The complexity of theorem-proving procedures. STOC. Public record.
